questions.question: Reserve Bank Innovation Hub (RBIH) was inaugurated in 2022 with an initial capital of Rs. _______.
questions.explanation:
• The Reserve Bank Innovation Hub (RBIH) was inaugurated by Shaktikanta Das in 2022. The wholly-owned subsidiary of RBI is intended to encourage and nurture financial innovation sustainably.
  • It was set up with an initial capital of Rs. 100 crores.
  • It will help bring world-class innovation to the financial sector. The RBIH is also working on the blueprint of the Digital Rupee.

questions.question: Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation or DICGC, which is a subsidiary of the RBI, was established in which year?
questions.explanation:
• DICGC, or Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation, is a specialised division of the RBI and works under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of Finance.
  • It was established in 1978 under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, of 1961 to provide insurance for deposits.
  • It ensures all bank deposits, saving, fixed, recurring, and current, up to an extent of Rs. 5 lakhs for each depositor in one bank.
  • The limit was Rs. 1 lakh earlier, but it was increased in February 2020.

questions.question: What is limit of maximum cover insured by DICGC?
questions.explanation:
• The DICGC insures principal and interest upto a maximum amount of ₹ 5 lakhs.
  • For example, if an individual had an account with a principal amount of 4,95,000 plus accrued interest of 4,000, the total amount insured by the DICGC would be 4,99,000.

questions.question: RBI maintains the Principal Accounts of Union as well as State governments at its Central Accounts Section in:
questions.explanation:
• RBI carries out the general banking business of the governments through its own offices and commercial banks, both public and private, appointed as its agents.
  • Section 45 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, provides for appointment of scheduled commercial banks as agents at all places or at any place in India, for purposes that it may specify, “having regard to public interest, convenience of banking, banking development and such other factors which in its opinion are relevant in this regard”.
  • Reserve Bank of India maintains the Principal Accounts of Central as well as State Governments at its Central Accounts Section, Nagpur.
  • It has put in place a well-structured arrangement for revenue collection as well as payments on behalf of Government across the country.
  • A network comprising the Government Banking Divisions of RBI and branches of agency banks appointed under Section 45 of the RBI Act carry out the government transactions.
  • At present all the public sector banks and select private sector banks act as RBI's agents. Only designated branches of agency banks can conduct government banking business.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements are correct with respect to Core Inflation?

  1. It is the change in the costs of goods and services and does not include food and energy sectors.
  2. It is considered as an indicator of long-term inflation.
  3. Core inflation is dominated by the transport and communication categories in India.

Choose the correct codes:
questions.explanation:
Correct Answer (A).

  • Core Inflation is measured as CPI inflation excluding food and fuel to avoid the impact of short-term volatility.

  • It is regarded as a long-term measure of underlying inflation trends, useful for monetary policy.

  • In India, core inflation is mainly influenced by housing, health, education, clothing, and other services.

  • Transport & communication has at times driven inflation spikes (e.g., telecom tariff hikes), but it is not structurally the dominant category.

questions.question: When the rise in price level is less than 3 percent per annum, it is known as ____________________.
questions.explanation: • When the rise in price level is less than 3 percent per annum, it is termed as creeping or mild inflation. The price of goods and services rise moderately, and it is usually considered helpful for the development of the economy.

questions.question: At present, how many fully owned subsidiaries of RBI are there?
questions.explanation:
There are 5 subsidiaries of RBI. They are-

  1. RBI Innovation Hub (RBIH)
  2. Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee of India (DICGI)
  3. Bhartiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Pvt Ltd (BRBNMPL)
  4. Reserve Bank Information Technology Pvt Ltd (ReBIT)
  5. Indian Financial Technology and Allied Services (IFTAS)

questions.question: How many  Central Board of Directors are there in RBI?
questions.explanation:
• RBI commenced its operations from 1st April 1935.
  • The Central Board of Directors is headed by the RBI Governor, comprising of 21 members  including the Governor. 4 Deputy Governor, 2 Finance Ministry representatives, 10 government nominated directors to represent important elements of Indian economy, 4 directors to represent local boards.

questions.question: Which of the following sections grants power to RBI to issue the currency?
questions.explanation:
• Section 22 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 grants power to RBI to issue the currency.
  • On the other hand, section 24 states that the highest denomination note could be Rs. 10,000.

questions.question: As per section 24 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, the highest denomination that the RBI can print note is of _______.
questions.explanation:
• Section 24 of the RBI Act, 1934 states that the highest denomination of notes can be Rs. 10,000.
  • Other important sections of the RBI Act:

(i) Section 24 grants power to RBI to issue the currency

(ii) Section 4 defines the capital of RBI, which is 5 crores of rupees.

(iii) Section 17 deals with the functioning of RBI.

  • It can accept deposits from the central and state governments without interest, and it can also buy or sell government securities.
  • RBI can purchase and discount bills of exchange from commercial banks.

(iv) Section 21 assigns RBI the duty of being a banker to the central government and a manager of public debt.

questions.question: What is the role of DICGC, a subsidiary of RBI?
questions.explanation:
• Here, the correct answer is (d).
  • The Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation (DICGC) is responsible for insuring deposits in banks, providing a safety net to depositors in case of bank failures.
  • DICGC is a subsidiary of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
  • It provides deposit insurance to protect bank deposit holders if the bank fails to pay its depositors
  • All types of deposit accounts (savings, current, recurring, and fixed deposits) are insured up to a limit of Rs. 5 lakh per account holder per bank
  • If an individual's deposit amount exceeds Rs. 5 lakh in a single bank, only Rs. 5 lakh, including principal and interest, will be paid by DICGC if the bank becomes bankrupt

questions.question: The directors of RBI are appointed for a _____ year  term.
questions.explanation:
• The main committee of the RBI is the central board of directors, who are appointed by the GoI for a 4-year term. The board includes the governor of RBI and not more than 4 deputy governors.
  • 4 directors represent the regional boards, 2 are from the Ministry of Finance (usually the Economic Affairs Secretary and the Financial Services Secretary), and 10 other directors are from various fields.
  • Shaktikanta Das is the current governor of RBI, while there are currently 4 deputy governors, Mahesh Kumar Jain, M. Rajeshwar Rao, Michael Patra, and T. Rabi Shankar.

questions.question: When did the Banking Regulation Act come into effect?
questions.explanation:
The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 is a key legislation in India that regulates all banking firms, including commercial banks and, later, co-operative banks.

  • Originally passed as the Banking Companies Act, 1949, it came into force on 16 March 1949.

  • It was renamed the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 later the same year (not in 1966).

  • It was made applicable to Jammu & Kashmir in 1956.

  • Initially, the Act applied only to banking companies (i.e., commercial banks).

  • In 1965, the Act was amended to make it applicable to co-operative banks.

  • The amended provisions came into effect on 1 July 1966, making this the key date for co-operative banks under the Act.

In 2020, the Act was further amended to strengthen regulation over urban co-operative banks, placing them under the direct supervision of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).

questions.question: When was ReBIT, a wholly-owned subsidiary of  RBI, formed?
questions.explanation:
• ReBIT stands for Reserve Bank Information Technology Private Limited, and it is a whollyowned subsidiary of RBI, formed in 2016.
  • It was set up by RBI for its IT and cybersecurity needs, and also to ensure the cyber resilience of Indian banking.  Prof. Sachin Chaturvedi is the Chairman of ReBIT.

questions.question: What is the primary function of the Reserve Bank Information Technology Private Limited (ReBIT), a subsidiary of RBI?
questions.explanation:
• Here, the correct answer is (b).
  • ReBIT focuses on developing and implementing information technology solutions for the RBI and the broader financial sector, enhancing efficiency and security.
  • It was established in 2016.
  • ReBIT's services include software development, data management, network management, security, and technical support.
  • The company also provides training and consulting services to help organizations improve their IT capabilities.

questions.question: What is the primary objective of the Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited (BRBNMPL), a subsidiary of RBI?
questions.explanation:
• Here, the correct answer is (B).
  • BRBNMPL is responsible for the printing and supply of currency notes in India, ensuring an adequate supply of currency in circulation.
  • It was established in 1995 to address the demand for banknotes and coins.
  • It supplies a major portion of banknote requirements in the country, while the remaining requirements are met through the Security Printing & Minting Corporation of India Limited (SPMCIL).

questions.question: What is the primary objective of the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI), an entity promoted by RBI?
questions.explanation:
• Here the correct answer is, is (c).
  • NPCI is responsible for the development and management of digital payment and settlement systems in India, promoting a cashless economy.
  • This includes operating banking networks and providing interoperable payment systems that enable consumers to make transactions across multiple banks.
  • NPCI also aims to promote financial inclusion and empower people to transact banking services through digital channels.
  • Additionally, NPCI works to increase the adoption of electronic payments and provide a secure and efficient payments platform for individuals and businesses.

questions.question: How many Zonal office does RBI have?
questions.explanation: RBI has 4 zonal offices & that ofice is known as local board. These offices are located at Mumbail, Chennai, Delhi and Kolkata.  Head of these zonal offices are known as Director. These 4 directors are a part of a BOARDS OF MEMBERS OF RBI.

questions.question: What does first C in DICGC stand for?
questions.explanation:
• DICGC stands for Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation is a wholly owned subsidiary of Reserve Bank of India.
  • It was established on 15 July 1978 under the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act, 1961 for the purpose of providing insurance of deposits and guaranteeing of credit facilities.

questions.question: Which of the following is the role of Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited (BRBNMPL)?
options: To design, deploy & support IT-related services to all Banks and Financial Institutions in the country.
To ensure cyber resilience of Indian banking.
To augment the production of bank notes in India.
To promote Financial Education across India.
questions.explanation:
Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited(BRBNMPL)

  • Establishment: Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited (BRBNMPL) was established by Reserve Bank of India (RBI) as its wholly-owned subsidiary on 3rd February 1995. The BRBNMPL has been registered as a Private Limited Company under the Companies Act 1956.
  • Role of BRBNMPL: To augment the production of bank notes in India to enable the RBI to bridge the gap between the supply and demand for banknotes in the country.
  • Headquarters: Bengaluru

Chairman: Shri T. Rabi Sankar

questions.question: The Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance was also known as the________.
questions.explanation:
• The Reserve Bank of India was set up on the basis of the recommendations of the Royal Commission on Indian Currency and Finance also known as the Hilton-Young Commission.
  • In 1926, Royal Commission on Indian Currency (Hilton Young Commission) recommends the establishment of a central bank to called the ‘Reserve Bank of India’.
  • Indian Central Banking Enquiry Committee revives the issue of the establishment of the Reserve Bank of India as the Central Bank for India.

questions.question: RBI provides WMA to state governments for a period of______.
questions.explanation:
• WMA is a facility for both the Centre and states to borrow from the RBI.
  • These borrowings are meant purely to help them to tide over temporary mismatches in cash flows of their receipts and expenditures. In that sense, they aren’t a source of finance per se.
  • Section 17(5) of the RBI Act, 1934 authorises the central bank to lend to the Centre and state governments subject to their being repayable “not later than three months from the date of the making of the advance”.

questions.question: When creeping and walking inflation are left unchecked, the rate of inflation will rise above 10% and it is termed as _________.
questions.explanation:
• When creeping and walking inflation are left unchecked, the rate of inflation will rise above 10% and hence, is termed as galloping inflation.
  • Galloping inflation is one that develops at a fast pace, but only for a brief period.
  • This form of inflation is dangerous for the economy as it mostly affects the middle and low-income classes of population.
  • It has the potential to trigger an economic downturn.

questions.question: The Banking Regulation Act is not applicable to which of the following?
questions.explanation:
• The Banking Regulation Act came into force on the 16th of March 1949. The Act was amended in 1965 by adding Section 56 to include cooperative banks under its purview.
  • The Act does not apply to Primary Agricultural Credit Societies and Cooperative Land Mortgage Banks.

questions.question: Who was the first Indian to be the governor of the Reserve Bank?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'C' that is 'CD Deshmukh'.
  • Chintaman Dwarkanath Deshmukh, a member of the Indian Civil Service, was the first Indian Governor of the RBI.

Key Facts: 

  • Chintaman Dwarkanath Deshmukh, a member of the Indian Civil Service, was the first Indian Governor of the Bank.
  • His association with the Bank commenced in 1939. He later served as Secretary and thereafter in 1941 as Deputy Governor of the Bank.
  • On the demise of James Taylor, he took over stewardship of the Bank and was appointed Governor in August 1943.
  • He later held the office of Union Finance Minister between 1950-56.

Additional Information: 

  • Sir James Taylor – British, Governor of RBI (1937–1943).
  • Sir Benegal Rama Rau – Indian, but later (1949–1957), the longest-serving RBI Governor.
  • P. C. Bhattacharya – Governor (1962–1967).
  • K. R. Puri – Governor (1975–1977).

questions.question: Which of the following statement/s is/ are correct with respect to the core inflation?
options: Food and energy prices are exempted from the calculation of core inflation.
It represents the long run trend in the price level.
It is less volatile than headline inflation
questions.explanation:
• Core Inflation is the price rise in all goods and services except food and energy due to high prices fluctuations is core inflation. It is calculated as government needs a stable and true picture of inflation. It represents the long run trend in the price level.
  • Food and energy prices are exempt from this calculation because their prices can be too volatile or fluctuate.
  • Headline inflation is a more volatile measure than core inflation.

questions.question: BRBNMPL is a specialised division of the Reserve Bank of India, which mints Indian banknotes and is under the ownership of the Ministry of Finance. What does ‘M’ in BRBNMPL stand for?
questions.explanation:
• Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran Private Limited is a subsidiary of RBI mints Indian bank notes.
  • It was established in 1995 to address the demand for banknotes and coins.
  • It supplies a major portion of banknote requirements in the country, while the remaining requirements are met through the Security Printing & Minting Corporation of India Limited (SPMCIL).

questions.question: Which deposits among the following are insured by DICGC?
questions.explanation:
• DICGC stands for Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation is a wholly owned subsidiary of Reserve Bank of India.
  • All types of deposits like savings deposits, term deposits and RDs are covered by DICGC. However, government and inter-bank deposits are not covered.  
  • Also, deposits of the state land development banks with the state co-operative bank are not covered.

questions.question: Under the Minimum Reserve System followed by  the RBI, it has to maintain assets of at least _____ at all times.
questions.explanation:
• The Minimum Reserve System (MRS) has been applicable in India since 1956. Under this system, RBI has to maintain assets of at least Rs. 200 crores at all times. Rs. 115 crores should be in the form of gold or gold bullion, and the rest Rs. 85 crores should be in the form of foreign currencies.
  • After the maintenance of this minimum reserve, the RBI can print currency notes as per the requirement of the economy with prior permission from the government.
  • The sole purpose of MRS is to maintain the money supply in the country’s economy without increasing inflation and also to maintain the confidence of the general public in the currency.

questions.question: National Centre for Financial Education is a Section 8 not-for-profit company promoted by RBI, SEBI, IRDAI, and PFRDA. The stake of RBI in NCFE
questions.explanation:
• NCFE or National Centre for Financial Education is a not-for-profit Section 8 company promoted by the Reserve Bank of India, the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India, and the Pension Fund Regulatory and Development Authority. RBI, SEBI, and IRDAI own a 30% stake while the PFRDA has a 10% stake in the company.
  • It was established to promote financial education across India as per the National Strategy for Financial Education (NSFE). Rs. 100 crores were the initial share capital of NCFE.

questions.question: RBI was constituted on the recommendation of which committee?
questions.explanation:
During the 1920s the Britishers felt the need of a central bank to manage the financial system of a country. In 1926 a committee was formulated to look upon the need of a Central Bank. This committee is known as Hilton Young Committee which was established under the chairmanship of Young Hilton. This commission is also known as Royal Commission. It laid its report in the British Parliament in 1927, but it was rejected by the British Legislatures.

Later the economic crisis of 1929-33 opened the window of a need of a Central Bank in India. Further in 1934, the RBI Act 1934 was passed and finally it led to the establishment of RBI at Calcutta, West Bengal in April 1935.

questions.question: When the prices rise on account of the deficit in the government expenditure and government looks for expansion of money and credit that results in inflation. This type of inflation is termed as?
questions.explanation:
• An economy faces deficit balance when its expenditures exceed revenue.
  • To meet this gap, the government prints more money through central bank.
  • So, price rise in the economy due to the government’s effort to level of the deficit balance is known as the deficit-induced inflation.

questions.question: The board of directors of RBI includes not more than _____ deputy governors.
questions.explanation:
• The central board of directors are the main committee of the RBI, and it should include not more than 4 deputy governors.
  • The directors are appointed by the government for not more than 4 years.
  • The board also includes the governor of RBI, 4 directors that represent the regional boards, 2 from the Ministry of Finance (usually the Economic Affairs Secretary and the Financial Services Secretary), and 10 other directors from various fields.

questions.question: Who was the first Governor of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI)?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'C' that is 'Osborne Smith'
  • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) was established on 1st April 1935.
  • Sir Osborne Arkell Smith (often written as Sir Osborne Smith) was appointed as the first Governor of RBI (1935–1937).

Key Information: 

  • Osborne Smit was a British banker and had earlier served as the Managing Governor of the Imperial Bank of India (now SBI).
  • After him, Sir James Taylor became the second Governor (1937–1943).
  • The first Indian Governor was C. D. Deshmukh (1943–1949).
  • So, while Osborn Smith was the first Governor overall, C. D. Deshmukh was the first Indian Governor.

questions.question: Which among the following currency printing press are fully owned by Government of India?
questions.explanation:
• India has four currency note printing presses.
  • The central government controls two of them - at Nashik in Maharashtra and Dewas in Madhya Pradesh.
  • While an RBI subsidiary, the Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran (P) Ltd controls the other two - at Mysuru in Karnataka and Salboni in West Bengal.

questions.question: When was ReBIT established?
questions.explanation: The RBI has set up Reserve Bank Information Technology Pvt Ltd (ReBIT)  in 2016. Its headquarter was at Mumbai, Maharastra. It was setup to meet it's  IT requirement, including the cyber security needs of the banks and its regulated entities.

questions.question: Reserve Bank of India established under which act?
questions.explanation:
• The Reserve Bank of India was established on April 1, 1935, in accordance with the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934.
  • The Central Office of the Reserve Bank was initially established in Kolkata but was permanently moved to Mumbai in 1937. The Central Office is where the Governor sits and where policies are formulated.
  • Though originally privately owned, since nationalization in 1949, the Reserve Bank is fully owned by the Government of India.

questions.question: How many branches does the RBI have in India?
questions.explanation:
• The correct answer is option 'B' that is 33.
  • The Reserve Bank of India has offices at 33 locations.
  • The RBI has 4 zonal offices in India, in Mumbai, Kolkata, Delhi and Chennai, while there are 19 regional offices.
  • The central office of the RBI is in Mumbai.
  • The Governor sits in the central office and the policies are also formulated in the central office.

questions.question: In which year, the Nationalization of the Reserve Bank of India was done?
questions.explanation:
• The Reserve Bank of India was nationalized with effect from 1st January 1949 on the basis of the Reserve Bank of India (Transfer to Public Ownership) Act, 1948.
  • All shares in the capital of the Bank were deemed transferred to the Central Government on payment of suitable compensation.
  • Established: 1 April 1935
  • Ownership: Ministry of Finance, Government of India

questions.question: How many currency Printing Press are there in India?
questions.explanation:
• India has four currency note printing presses.
  • The central government controls two of them - at Nashik in Maharashtra and Dewas in Madhya Pradesh.
  • While an RBI subsidiary, the Bharatiya Reserve Bank Note Mudran (P) Ltd controls the other two - at Mysuru in Karnataka and Salboni in West Bengal.

questions.question: Which of the following financial institutions Regulate The Foreign Exchange Market, Government Securities Market, and Money Market ?
questions.explanation:
• The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the central bank of India. It is responsible for regulating the financial system in India, including the foreign exchange market, government securities market, and money market.

  • Foreign Exchange Market: The Foreign Exchange Management Act 1999 came into light after the liberalization measures introduced in 1991. FEMA 1991 replaced the FERA 1973 and came into effect in June 2022.

  • So now, the RBI is responsible for overseeing the foreign exchange market in India. RBI supervises and regulates the Foreign Exchange Market through the provision of the FEMA Act 1999.

  • Government Securities Market: RBI regulates the trade securities issued by the Central and State governments. For regulation of this, RBI derives its power from the RBI Act of 1934.

  • Money Market: Short-term and highly liquid debt securities are also regulated by RBI and for this RBI derives its powers from the RBI Act 1934.

questions.question: Which of the following functions of RBI describes the main objective of changing this cash reserve ratio by the RBI is to control credit?
questions.explanation:
• As bankers’ bank, the RBI holds a part of the cash reserves of commercial banks and lends them funds for short periods.

  • All banks are required to maintain a certain percentage (lying between 3 per cent and 15 per cent) of their total liabilities.

  • The main objective of changing this cash reserve ratio by the RBI is to control credit.

questions.question:
Choose the correct statement regarding the functions of RBI:

  1. Regulator of Bank and Development Authority

  2. Regulator of NBFC

  3. Lender of Last Resort

  4. Banker’s Bank

  5. Regulator of Open Market Operations
questions.explanation:
• The RBI regulates the banking system by setting capital adequacy requirements, liquidity requirements, and other prudential norms. The RBI also monitors the activities of banks to ensure that they are not engaged in any risky activities.

  • The RBI regulates NBFCs to ensure that they are safe and sound. The RBI regulates NBFCs by setting capital adequacy requirements, liquidity requirements, and other prudential norms. The RBI also monitors the activities of NBFCs to ensure that they are not engaged in any risky activities.

  • The RBI is the lender of last resort for the banking system. This means that the RBI will lend money to banks that are in financial difficulty. The RBI provides loans to banks at a concessional rate of interest. The RBI's role as lender of last resort helps to prevent bank runs and financial instability.

  • The RBI is the banker's bank. This means that commercial banks hold their reserves with the RBI. The RBI also provides clearing and settlement services to commercial banks. The RBI's role as banker's bank helps ensure the banking system's smooth functioning.

  • The RBI is the regulator of open market operations. Open market operations are the buying and selling of government securities by the RBI. The RBI uses open market operations to control the money supply in the economy. The RBI's role as regulator of open market operations helps to ensure that the money supply is in line with the RBI's monetary policy objectives.

questions.question: There cannot be more than ____________ Deputy Governors in the Reserve Bank of India.
questions.explanation:
• Official Directors (central board of directors)
  • Full-time: Governor and not more than four Deputy Governors
  • Non-Official Directors
  • Nominated by Government: ten Directors from various fields and two government Official
  • Others: four Directors - one each from four local boards (regional)

questions.question: Which function of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is reflected when it changes the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) to control the flow of credit in the economy?
options: Exchange Management and Control
questions.explanation:
• The Correct answer is option 'C' that is 'Controller of Credit'.
  • Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) is a monetary policy tool used by the RBI.
  • By increasing or decreasing the CRR, RBI can control the amount of money banks can lend, thereby controlling credit and liquidity in the economy.
  • This action comes under the "Controller of Credit" function of the RBI.

questions.question: Which of the following statements are correct regarding the RBI's function “Banker to the Government”?
options: Accepts and pays money on behalf of the  Government.
It carries out exchange remittances and  other banking operations.
RBI provides short-term credit to the  Government of India.
questions.explanation:
• The RBI acts as the banker to the government of India and State Governments (except Jammu and Kashmir). As such it transacts all banking business of these Govern­ments.
  • Accepts and pays money on behalf of the Government.
  • It carries out exchange remittances and other banking operations.
  • As the Government’s banker, the RBI provides short-term credit to the Government of India.
  • This short-term credit is obtainable through the sale of treasury bills. Not only this, but the RBI also provides ways and means of advances (repayable within 90- days) to the State Government.
  • It may be noted that the Central Government is empowered to borrow any amount it likes from the RBI.

questions.question: Under which function of RBI, is it described that RBI not only regulates the currency and credit but also aids the development of the Indian economy by conducting various types of promotional activities?
questions.explanation:
• Apart from these traditional functions, the RBI performs various activities of a promotional and developmental nature. 
  • It attempts to mobilize savings for productive purposes. This is done in various ways. 
  • For instance, RBI has helped a lot in building the huge financial infrastructure that we see now.
  • Thus, it is clear that RBI is not a typical Cen­tral Bank as is traditionally understood. It is something more than a Central Bank. 
  • It regulates not only currency and credit but aids the development of the Indian economy by conducting various types of promotional activities. As such, in RBI we see many activities combined into one.

questions.question: Which of the following functions of RBI has given the author­ity to enter into foreign exchange transactions both on its own account and on behalf of the Govern­ment?
options: Promotional and Developmental Functions
questions.explanation:
• One of the essential central banking functions performed by the Bank is that of maintaining the external value of rupee. 
  • The external stability of the currency is closely related to its internal stability the inherent economic strength of the country and the way it con­ducts its economic and monetary affairs.
  • Domestic, fiscal and monetary policies have, therefore, an im­portant role in maintaining the external value of the currency. 
  • Reserve Bank of India has a very impor­tant role to play in this area.

questions.question: Which of the following Financial Institution Issues currency in India?
questions.explanation:
• The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the sole authority to issue currency notes in India. It also prints coins and regulates the supply of currency in the economy.

  • Printing currency notes: The RBI prints currency notes at its currency printing presses in Nashik, Dewas, and Mysore.

  • Issuing currency notes: The RBI issues currency notes through its offices all over India.

  • Withdrawing currency notes: The RBI withdraws currency notes from circulation when they become worn or damaged.

  • Replacing currency notes: The RBI replaces currency notes that are lost or stolen.

  • Destroying currency notes: The RBI destroys currency notes no longer fit for circulation.

  • Monitoring the supply of currency: The RBI monitors the supply of currency in the economy to ensure that it is adequate to meet the needs of the people.

  • The RBI's role in issuing currency is important because it helps to ensure that the Indian rupee is a stable and reliable currency. The RBI's role also helps to promote financial inclusion by making it easier for people to access currency.

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding the roles played by RBI is correct?
options: It is the Bank of Issue
It acts as a banker to the Government
It is the banker of other banks
It regulates the flow of credit
questions.explanation: • The Reserve Bank of India, as the central bank of the country, functions as the sole bank with the right of issuing paper notes, it acts as banker to the Government, it is the banker to other bank and it regulates the flow of credit
